analysis.one_liner: Lets doctors refer their own Medicare patients to hospitals they partially own again.
analysis.headline: The bill never came up for a vote in either committee and expired at the end of the 117th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law currently bars doctors from sending their Medicare patients to hospitals in which they have an ownership stake, with a narrow exception for hospitals that existed before 2010. This bill would repeal the restrictions added by the Affordable Care Act that limit that exception, so doctors could once again build or expand physician-owned hospitals and treat their own patients there. Supporters frame this as expanding patient choice and competition; critics of self-referral have long argued it leads to more tests and procedures and higher Medicare spending.
analysis.who_benefits: Doctors who invest in, build, or expand physician-owned hospitals, and the management companies that operate them. Those physicians would regain the ability to own hospitals and refer their own patients to them for Medicare-paid care.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Physician owners and investors in hospitals

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals ACA provisions that limit physician self-referrals at newly built or expanded physician-owned hospitals, restoring the pre-2010 exception to the self-referral ban [S2].
The full text repeals sections 6001 and 10601 of the ACA and section 1106 of the 2010 reconciliation act, and restores the law as if those changes had never been enacted [S3].
Supporters characterize physician-owned hospitals as higher quality, arguing the bill would give patients more options and increase competition [S1].

analysis.who_pays: Medicare and its beneficiaries, if self-referral again increases the volume of physician-ordered scans, procedures, and admissions at facilities the referring doctors own. Community hospitals that cannot self-refer would also face losing cases to physician-owned competitors.

drawbacks.text: Physicians who profit from the facilities they refer to have a financial incentive to order more services and to favor profitable patients; Congress restricted self-referral under the Stark law for exactly this reason, and the ACA provisions this bill repeals were that restriction's enforcement teeth [S2].

Easing self-referral limits would let physician-owned hospitals draw paying cases away from community hospitals, which serve emergency and charity cases and could see their payer mix worsen as profitable cases move out.
The bill carries no new quality or disclosure requirements, so nothing in it ties the restored referral rights to patient protections.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers doctors with hospital investments a large financial opportunity, and some physician-owned hospitals do post strong quality scores. But it removes a safeguard whose purpose is to keep doctors' medical judgments separate from their ownership stakes, and the likely cost shows up as more Medicare-paid services and a strained community-hospital system. On balance the transfer runs from Medicare and ordinary patients to physician owners, with no compensating protections in the text.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in committee after being referred to Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and the Health subcommittee, and neither committee ever took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 25, 2021 and referred the same day to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees, and then to the Health subcommittee [S5].
No hearing, markup, or vote appears in the action history; the bill's last recorded action is its referral in February 2021 [S5].
The bill attracted 38 cosponsors, 35 Republicans and 3 Democrats, and died without floor action when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Medicare beneficiaries and community hospitals keep the existing limits on physician self-referral; the physician-owned hospital industry did not get the expanded referral rights it sought.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Patients and community hospitals kept the limits

industries.note: The bill would restore these doctors' legal right to refer their own Medicare patients to hospitals they own, reopening a profitable channel closed by the ACA. Referring doctors profit when more services are ordered, which is why the referral ban exists.

Physician-owned facilities tend to draw profitable, well-insured cases, leaving community hospitals with more emergency and charity care. Hospitals' interest in keeping those cases partly runs alongside patients' interest in the existing referral limits.
These companies operate physician-owned facilities and would gain new building and expansion opportunities if the referral limits were repealed.
